To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
language is a mediator of executive function in deaf children.

Deaf children performed less well on nonverbal executive function tasks, even when controlling for nonverbral IQ and processing speed, and language mediated executive function performance, but the reverse was not true.
language is key in nonverbal EF performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between language and cognitive abilities.
the development of executive functions in typically developing children, and in particular the relationship between executive functions and language.
the development and assessment of nonverbal Executive Functions (EF) in deaf and hearing children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nonverbal executive function is mediated by language, but language is not mediated by nonverbal executive functions.
nonverbal executive function is mediated by language.
the development of EF skills is dependent upon the development of language skills, and that language skills are the key factor in the development of EF.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between language and EF is mediated by the language.
the development of executive functions is dependent on the development of language, and that language is the most important factor in the development of executive functioning.
language is a necessary but not sufficient condition for EF skill.
The main takeaway from our work is that
language is a critical component of nonverbal executive function.
language plays a crucial role in EF performance, and this is true even for children with deafness, a group in which language is not a product of cognition.
the relationship between language and executive function is not a two-way street.
